messages.content:
Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Generator scaffolding left in: oaicite, [cite: 1], placeholders -- finish the text and read it
- The "it's not X, it's Y" construction -- just state Y
- A bolded word opening a list item as a per-item tag -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- Saying "is" the long way: serves as, boasts, functions as -- use the plain verb
- One-line dramatic fragments: "That's it. That's the whole thing." -- cut them, the preceding sentence already made the point
- Em dashes clustering in one document -- most drafts need 0-2; use commas, periods or parentheses for the rest
- Filler verbs: leverages, facilitates, unlocks -- use a plain verb, or cut the sentence
- A snake_case identifier written as plain prose -- name it in words, or mark it as inline code
- Marketing cliches: "hidden gem", "let's dive in" -- say the specific thing
- The "Not X. Not Y." listing construction -- state the point once
- Stock section skeleton: "Despite its success", "Looking ahead" -- name the specific thing the section is for
- Standalone filler adverbs: undoubtedly, arguably, notably, importantly, ultimately -- most add nothing; cut them unless one is carrying real emphasis
- A banned synonym of one of this project's canonical terms, per its declared lexicon -- one word, one meaning: use the canonical term the word's own note names
- Dramatic turning points with nothing concrete behind them: "Everything changed." -- name the actual event, or cut it

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the About page for a company that makes scheduling software for medical clinics. Around 250 words.

# About Us

We started Corvid Health in 2017 after spending three years building intake software for a hospital network in Ohio. The clinics we worked with had the same complaint every time: the schedule was the thing everyone fought about. Front desk staff kept a paper backup because the system lied to them. Physicians found out about double-bookings at 8:05 in the morning. Nobody trusted the screen.

So we built a scheduler that tells the truth about what a clinic day actually looks like. Rooms, equipment, provider credentials, and interpreter availability all get treated as real constraints, because they are. When a patient books a 40-minute visit that needs an ultrasound room and a Spanish-speaking provider, our software either finds that slot or says plainly that it does not exist.

Today we serve 340 clinics across 18 states, mostly independent practices and community health centers between four and sixty providers. We are 31 people, about half of us in Columbus and the rest scattered. Eleven of our staff worked in a clinic before they worked here, which is why our support line is answered by someone who knows what a no-show rate does to a Tuesday.

We charge per provider per month. No implementation fee, no per-message billing, no separate line item for the patient reminders that make the whole thing work. Clinics can export their full schedule history at any time, in a format they can read without us.

We are privately held and profitable. We plan to stay both.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.

- paragraph_uniformity (4 paragraphs, spread 0.17):

Return only the rewritten text.
